resources.string: Survival Guide
FIELD
DIGITAL
Field & Emergency Survival
Digital & OpSec Survival
Open-source field manual — verify locally, train before you need it
Emergency Communications
Signal discipline, radio basics and the rule of three
The universal distress signal is three of anything: three whistle blasts, three fires, three light flashes. Repeat in cycles with pauses — searchers are trained to recognize it.

Agree on a radio channel, call schedule and fallback frequencies with your team before separation. Key the mic, speak clearly, end with \"over\". A phone is a radio too — offline maps and GPS work without signal.
Signal mirrors, whistles and bright cloth are cheap, weightless backups that never run out of battery. A mirror flash is visible for kilometers in daylight.
Water Sourcing & Treatment
Find it, filter it, boil it — the 3-day rule
You can survive 3 weeks without food but only 3 days without water. Prioritize water above everything except shelter in extreme weather.
Boiling is the most reliable treatment: 1 minute rolling boil at sea level, 3 minutes above 2000 m. Filter cloudy water through cloth first, then boil or use purification tablets.
Find water downhill: valleys, lines of green vegetation, animal trails converging, morning dew on grass. Rain collection and solar stills are slow but work.
Shelter
The rule of 3s: 3 hours without shelter in extreme conditions
3 minutes without air, 3 hours without shelter in extreme conditions, 3 days without water, 3 weeks without food. Shelter beats fire and water in cold, wind or wet weather.
Pick high ground away from water, falling branches and wind tunnels. Insulate from the ground — a thick leaf bed beats a thin blanket; you lose more heat to the ground than to the air.
A lean-to with a reflective wall (space blanket) doubles fire heat. Keep the entrance small and angled away from wind. Dry clothes are part of the shelter.
Fire
Tinder, kindling, fuel — the three-layer structure
Fire needs three layers: tinder (dry grass, birch bark, cotton), kindling (twigs), fuel (branches). Prepare twice as much of each as you think you need before striking a spark.
Ignition without matches: ferro rod sparks, battery + steel wool, a magnifier or a polished can bottom with sunlight. Carry at least two independent ignition methods.
In rain, split dead standing wood — the core stays dry. Store tinder in a waterproof bag always, not just when it rains.
Field First Aid
Stop bleeding, splint, rewarm — ABC first

ABC: Airway, Breathing, Circulation. Check responsiveness, clear the airway, verify breathing, then stop major bleeding with direct pressure — not a tourniquet unless the limb is lost or pressure fails.
Splint fractures as found — do not straighten. Immobilize the joint above and below. Elevate sprains and apply cold if available.
Hypothermia kills faster than most injuries. Rewarm gradually: dry clothes, warm drinks (if conscious), shared body heat — never rub limbs or use direct heat on skin.
The 10 Essentials
Navigation, sun, insulation, light, first aid, fire, repair, food, water, shelter
The ten essentials: navigation (map + compass), sun protection, insulation, illumination, first-aid kit, fire starter, repair kit, food, water, emergency shelter.
Carry them on your person, not in a pack you might drop. A knife, cord and tape are the universal repair trio.
Keep cash, a paper contact list and a charged power bank — electronics fail exactly when you need them most.
Anonymous Communications
Tor, Signal, and identity separation
Use Tor (or the Tails live system) for anonymous browsing and Signal for end-to-end encrypted messaging. Never mix anonymous identities with your real accounts on the same device.
A burner device with no SIM history, paid in cash, is the baseline for operations that must not trace back. Assume every cell tower records your IMSI and location.
Metadata kills: who you talk to, when and how often is often more revealing than content. Use signal delays, vary timing and avoid patterns.
Device Anti-Forensics
Encrypt, wipe, isolate — before seizure, not after
Full-disk encryption with a long passphrase is the first line. After reboot, memory-based secrets (keys in RAM) decay — reboot or shut down when crossing borders or approaching checkpoints.
A Faraday bag blocks all radio: cellular, Wi-Fi, GPS tracking. Test it before relying on it — cheap bags leak.
Secure deletion means overwriting or crypto-erasing, not \"delete\". Deleting only removes the index entry; data survives until overwritten.
Bug & Camera Sweep
RF spectrum, IR glint, physical inspection
Hidden cameras reveal themselves by lens glint: sweep a strong light or IR flashlight in a dark room and look for pinpoint reflections (a phone camera sees IR).
RF bugs emit when transmitting. Use a spectrum sweep (this app\'s RF Sense) near suspect fixtures — smoke detectors, chargers, wall plates — and watch for unexpected signals.
Physical inspection: open fixtures, check for new holes, mismatched screws, unexpected wires. A bug needs power and a signal path — trace both.
Passwords & Authentication
Passphrases, a manager, 2FA — never reuse
Use a password manager and memorize only its master passphrase — five or more random words beat a short complex string and are easier to remember.
Enable 2FA everywhere; TOTP apps beat SMS (SIM-swap attacks). Keep recovery codes offline on paper.
Never reuse passwords across sites — one breached site compromises all. Check breach databases and rotate compromised credentials immediately.
Social Engineering Defense
Verify out-of-band, slow down, question urgency
Scammers weaponize urgency and authority. Any request demanding immediate action (payment, password, code) should trigger a full stop and out-of-band verification.
Verify identity out-of-band: hang up and call the known number, or use a pre-arranged code phrase. Never give sensitive information to someone who called you.
Phishing indicators: mismatched domains, urgent threats, generic greetings, requests to bypass normal process. Hover links, check headers, and when in doubt — don\'t click.
Digital Bug-Out Bag
3-2-1 backups, offline copies, rehearsed restore
3-2-1: three copies, two different media, one off-site. Encrypt backups before they leave your control — an unencrypted drive is a liability.
Keep an offline copy of critical documents (IDs, contacts, keys) in an encrypted container on a small drive, plus paper copies of the essentials.
A backup you haven\'t restored is a wish, not a plan. Rehearse a restore on a spare device once a year and verify the passphrase actually opens it.
Combat Trauma First Aid
Tourniquet, wound packing, tension pneumothorax

Massive bleeding is the number one preventable cause of battlefield death. Limb bleeding: place the tourniquet high (5–8 cm above the wound), tighten until bleeding stops, note the time — professional care is required within 2 hours.
Junctional areas (armpit, groin, neck) cannot take a tourniquet — pack the wound with hemostatic gauze and hold direct pressure for 3+ minutes, then apply a pressure bandage.

Tension pneumothorax: chest penetrating wound plus progressive difficulty breathing requires needle decompression (2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular line). If untrained, seek guidance — do not improvise blind.
CBRN Protection
Upwind evacuation, sealing, decontamination
Determine wind direction and move upwind / crosswind. Indoors: close windows and doors, shut ventilation, seal gaps with tape and plastic.
Decontamination order: remove outer clothing first (80% of contamination is on clothes), then rinse skin with large amounts of water, then change into clean clothes. No conditioner, no hot water.
Iodine tablets only protect against radioactive iodine and must be taken promptly; they do not block other radiation. N95 / gas masks stop inhalation but not every gas.
Camouflage & Concealment
Thermal signature, movement discipline, anti-tracking
Modern sensors see heat and movement. Night movement: slow, low, quiet — use vegetation and terrain shadows, never silhouette against the skyline.
Thermal management: a thermal blanket temporarily reduces heat signature; hide behind thick walls or rocks; a vehicle engine bay is the hottest signature around.
Anti-tracking: randomize routes, avoid fixed schedules, watch for the same vehicle or person appearing three times behind you, check reflective surfaces at night.
Food & Water Storage
Long-term reserves, rationing, calorie density
Long-term storage: minimum 2 L water and 2000 kcal per person per day; stock 3 days to 2 weeks and rotate stock regularly.
Rationing: when resupply is uncertain, ration from day one; protein goes to the weak first; water outranks food.
Emergency food: high-calorie, long-shelf-life (cans, energy bars, honey, nuts); avoid high-salt items that increase thirst.
Navigation & Escape Routes
Two routes minimum, no-GPS navigation, checkpoints
Plan at least two escape routes (on foot / by vehicle) avoiding bridges, tunnels and checkpoints; pre-set rendezvous points along each.
Navigation without GPS: map and compass; sun by day, North Star / Southern Cross by night; rivers flow toward population downstream.
Movement logging: record position every 30 minutes; tell a trusted person your route and timeline; agree on an overdue alarm protocol.
Signaling & Rescue
Ground-to-air signals, beacons, rescue discipline
Ground-to-air signals: SOS with rocks or trenches (3–10 m letters, high contrast); three fires in a line; mirror flashes at aircraft.
Electronic rescue: register a PLB / satellite beacon and trigger it once; in many countries 112 works even without a SIM card.
When rescue arrives: do not move the injured; wave bright clothing; at night draw slow circles with a light; stay in place and wait.
Communication Resilience
Grid-down comms, listening windows, paper redundancy
When power and cellular networks fail: two-way radios (agreed frequencies and callsigns), satellite messaging, mesh networks — and paper records.
Pre-arrange: an emergency frequency list, fixed listening windows (e.g. 5 minutes at the top of every hour), and a code-word list.
Information redundancy: write critical contacts on waterproof paper — never rely on a phone alone.
Location Privacy & Anti-Tracking
Silence devices, border discipline, cash habits
Smart devices are moving beacons: when silence matters, disable location, Bluetooth and Wi-Fi — or use a Faraday bag.
Borders and checkpoints: power off in advance (memory keys decay), separate devices among carriers, carry a clean \"white\" phone.
Cash discipline: buy sensitive supplies with cash, skip loyalty cards, never buy sensitive items at the same store on a schedule.
Emergency Power
Tiered power, solar selection, battery safety
Tier your power: small (phone/radio: power banks + solar panels), medium (lights/medical: portable power stations), large (generators — mind carbon monoxide ventilation).
Solar panels: folding panels are portable; overcast days deliver only 10–30% output; charge multiple power banks simultaneously.
Battery safety: keep lithium batteries out of direct sun and pressure; run generators 5+ meters from shelter, never indoors.
Psychological Resilience
Breathing control, team first aid, sleep discipline
Under crisis the brain enters fight / flight / freeze. 4-7-8 breathing (inhale 4 s, hold 7 s, exhale 8 s) rapidly calms the physiological alarm.
Team psychological first aid: listen without judgment, secure basics (water, food, sleep), assign simple tasks to restore a sense of control.
Sleep discipline: rotate watch so everyone gets at least 4 continuous hours per 24 h; caffeine only for critical windows.
Medical Information Card
Paper card, encrypted copy, medication backup
Paper emergency card: blood type, allergies, chronic conditions, medications, emergency contacts — one in wallet, one in pack.
Keep an encrypted digital copy and tell at least one companion how to open it; battlefield medicine does not wait while you unlock a phone.
Medication backup: at least 30 days of chronic medication, split between two locations — losing one cache leaves another.
Tiered Bug-Out Bag
EDC, 72-hour bag, long-term reserves
EDC (on person): knife, flashlight, lighter, cash, whistle, tourniquet, multitool.
72-hour bag: 3 L water + filter, 3 days food, shelter (emergency blanket / tarp), first-aid kit, comms, spare clothing.
Long-term / home reserves: two weeks of food and water, fuel, generator, medication, copies of key documents — inspect and rotate regularly.
OPERATING STEPS
CRITICAL WARNINGS

1. Fix frequencies before separating: agree primary + backup channels and callsigns, write on a waterproof card. 2. Any distress starts with the rule of three: 3 whistle blasts / 3 flashes / 3 fires, repeated in cycles with 1-minute gaps. 3. Radio discipline: press PTT, wait 1 second, speak slowly and clearly, end every transmission with \"over\". 4. Listening windows: monitor for 5 minutes at the top of every hour. 5. Phone as radio: pre-download offline maps — GPS works with zero signal; use airplane mode to save battery. 6. Get high for range: move to high ground or open terrain; do not block the antenna with your body. 7. Signal mirror: hold mirror in one hand, make a V over the target with the other, flash 3 times per group.

Radio direction-finding is real: in wartime, long transmissions expose your position — send short bursts and move. Sound carries far at night — it also gives you away. Use light signals when possible. Battery is ammunition: power off during non-critical hours.

1. Find water downhill: valley floors, lines of green vegetation, converging animal trails, rock hollows. 2. Collect in order of safety: rain > dew > flowing clear water > still water; take flowing water upstream of contamination. 3. Filter murky water through cloth, then sand, then charcoal in layers. 4. BOIL: rolling boil 1 minute (3 minutes above 2000 m). Boiling is the gold standard — do it whenever possible. 5. Chemical backup: purification tablets per instructions (usually 30 min); or 2 drops of 2% iodine per liter, wait 30 minutes. 6. Store 3 L per person per day; keep containers dark and covered to prevent algae.

Never drink from still water near animal carcasses or downstream of them. Melted snow must be boiled — cold does not kill pathogens. Seawater kills faster than thirst — it accelerates dehydration. Dark urine means you are already dehydrated. Drink before you feel thirst.

1. Site selection: high ground, out of wind, away from dead branches, riverbeds and cliff bases. 2. Insulate the ground first: a 30 cm bed of leaves/grass — the ground steals more heat than the air. 3. Lean-to: one ridge pole + angled poles at 45°, opening facing away from wind, reflective layer facing the fire. 4. Thatch the roof with leaves/moss laid pointing downward so water runs off. 5. Keep the entrance small — just big enough to crawl through — and hang a wind curtain. 6. Change out of wet clothes before sleeping; stuff them into the sleeping bag as extra insulation.
Never shelter in valley bottoms (cold air sinks) or dry riverbeds (flash floods). Keep fire at least 1.5 m from the shelter. Protect heat-loss zones first: head, neck, armpits, groin.

1. Prepare three layers before striking a spark: one fist of tinder (dry grass, birch bark, cotton), one armful of twigs, one pile of branches — double what you estimate. 2. Lay: cone style for wet/windy weather; log-cabin style for cooking. 3. Ferro rod: scrape at 45° with the knife spine, sparks onto the tinder. 4. Battery + steel wool: short two cells in series against the wool. 5. Magnifier or polished can bottom: focus to the smallest brightest point and hold still. 6. Nurture: when tinder smokes, blow gently; feed twigs first, then branches.

Keep tinder in a waterproof bag at all times, not just when it rains. In rain, split dead standing wood — the core is dry. Clear 1 m of ground around the fire; fully extinguish before leaving (water + soil, test with the back of your hand).

1. Assess: tap shoulders and shout; no response — call for help, check airway and breathing. 2. Stop massive bleeding with direct pressure: gauze + both hands, do not release for 10 minutes. 3. Limb arterial bleeding: tourniquet high on the limb (5–8 cm above wound), tighten until bleeding stops, write the time on it. 4. Fractures: splint in the position found — never straighten; immobilize the joints above and below. 5. Hypothermia: move out of wind/wet, dry clothing, warm the core (chest/back), warm drinks if conscious. 6. Shock: lay flat, raise legs 30 cm, keep warm, give nothing by mouth (especially abdominal wounds).

Never pull out an impaled object — stabilize it in place. Never give water to an unconscious person. Tourniquet window is 2 hours — mark the time, hand over to medical. Rubbing frostbitten tissue causes amputation.

1. Carry the ten essentials on your PERSON, not in a pack you might drop: navigation (map+compass), sun protection, insulation, illumination, first aid, fire, repair, food, water, emergency shelter. 2. Layer the load: EDC on body, 72-hour bag on back, long-term reserves at base. 3. Repair trio everywhere: knife, cord, tape. 4. Waterproof everything twice: double bags. 5. Drill monthly: use each item once so you know it works.
Gear you have not practiced with is gear you do not have. A broken compass beats a dead phone. In wartime, dark/olive gear over bright colors — visibility kills.

1. Build a Tails live USB from the official site (verify the signature) for anonymous sessions. 2. Use Tor Browser for anonymous browsing; never maximize the window. 3. Signal for end-to-end encrypted messaging with disappearing messages. 4. Separate anonymous identities from real ones: different devices, different accounts, never mixed. 5. Burner phone: bought with cash, no real-name registration, only public Wi-Fi at changing locations. 6. Compartmentalize: one identity per purpose; one leak must not chain to the rest.
Metadata kills: who you talk to, when, and how often reveals more than content. One single cross-login burns the whole identity. Public cameras see your face — anonymity is not just software.

1. Enable full-disk encryption with a long passphrase on every device. 2. Reboot or power off before borders, checkpoints or seizure risk — memory keys decay after reboot. 3. Test your Faraday bag: inside it, calls and GPS must fail completely. 4. Secure erase = overwrite (3 passes) or crypto-erase, never \"delete\". 5. Crossing borders: power off in advance, split devices between carriers, carry a clean \"white\" phone.
\"Deleted\" files survive until overwritten. Encryption does not stop coercion — plan what you will say. Cloud backups are a second crime scene.

1. Darken the room and sweep with a strong flashlight or IR light — look for pinpoint lens reflections (a phone camera sees IR). 2. Run an RF sweep (this app\'s RF Sense) against suspect fixtures: smoke detectors, chargers, wall plates, clocks, picture frames. 3. Physical inspection: open fixtures, look for new holes, mismatched screws, unexpected wires. 4. Power test: cut power — if the signal disappears it is wired; if not, it has a battery. 5. Pay special attention to gifts, borrowed devices and newly \"repaired\" items.

Do not talk about sensitive matters during or after the sweep — if you missed one, it heard you. Laser window-bounce surveillance exists — close curtains for sensitive discussions. A clean sweep is never a guarantee.

1. Use a password manager; memorize only its master passphrase: 5+ random words. 2. Enable TOTP 2FA everywhere; keep recovery codes on paper offline. 3. Give critical accounts (mail, bank, comms) unique strong passphrases. 4. Check breach databases regularly; rotate compromised credentials immediately. 5. Never share passwords or 2FA codes with anyone — no legitimate support asks.
SMS 2FA can be defeated by SIM-swap attacks. Phishing pages harvest 2FA codes in real time. Biometrics can be forced by anyone holding your finger or face.

1. Any request combining urgency + authority triggers a full stop — no legitimate emergency works this way. 2. Verify out-of-band: hang up and call the known number, or use a pre-arranged code phrase. 3. Never give sensitive information to someone who called YOU. 4. Inspect before clicking: hover links, check domains and sender headers. 5. Insider defense: least-knowledge principle, verify identity by behavior not appearance. 6. Slow down: real decisions can survive 10 minutes of checking.
Scammers manufacture urgency to disable your judgment. A hijacked account of someone you trust is the most dangerous vector. One careless click can compromise everything.

1. Follow 3-2-1: three copies, two different media, one off-site. 2. Encrypt backups (Veracrypt / Cryptomator) before they leave your control. 3. Keep paper copies of essential documents in two locations. 4. Rehearse a full restore on a spare device once a year. 5. Share the decryption passphrase with at least one trusted person.
A backup you have never restored is a wish, not a plan. Flash drives and disks fail without warning. Cloud storage is someone else\'s server.

1. Firefight first: return fire / reach cover before treating casualties — a dead medic helps no one. 2. Run MARCH: Massive bleeding → Airway → Respiration → Circulation → Hypothermia. 3. Limb bleeding: tourniquet high (5–8 cm above wound), tighten until bleeding stops, write the time; window is 2 hours. 4. Junctional wounds (armpit/groin/neck): pack with hemostatic gauze, hold pressure 3+ minutes, then pressure bandage. 5. Tension pneumothorax (chest wound + worsening breathing): needle decompression, 2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular line. 6. Evacuation: drag low-profile first; spinal injuries need a rigid board.
Never loosen a tourniquet once applied — that is a medical decision. Never remove impaled objects. Hypothermia kills faster than blood loss in cold conditions — treat both together.

1. Determine wind direction (grass, smoke, dust) and move upwind / crosswind immediately. 2. Indoors: close windows, doors and ventilation; tape and plastic over gaps; move to the innermost room. 3. Decontaminate in order: remove outer clothing (80% of contamination) → flush skin with large amounts of water → change into clean clothes. 4. Respiratory protection: N95 as an emergency stopgap; gas mask with the correct filter canister. 5. Iodine tablets: only against radioactive iodine, taken as early as possible. 6. Nerve agent signs (salivation, pinpoint pupils, convulsions): get away, ventilate, do not become the next casualty.

Nuclear flash: never look at it; drop flat, stay down 30+ seconds for the shockwave; shelter 48 hours if downwind. Hot water and conditioner accelerate chemical absorption — use cool water only. Removing clothing decontaminates more than any rinse.

1. Movement discipline: slow, low, quiet; move through shadows, never along the skyline. 2. Break your outline: vegetation, netting, local materials. 3. Thermal management: thermal blanket, thick walls, rock cover; let hot vehicle engines cool. 4. Anti-tracking: randomize routes, change schedules, watch for the same vehicle or person appearing three times. 5. Night adaptation: 20 minutes in darkness before moving; use red light for all tasks.
Movement is the most detectable thing you do. Drones see heat signatures — cover does not mean hidden. Reflections (watch, glasses, metal) are fatal at night.

1. Stock baseline: 2 L water + 2000 kcal per person per day, minimum 3 days, aim 2 weeks. 2. Ration from day one when resupply is uncertain; water outranks food. 3. Rotate stock: first in, first out; inspect every 6 months. 4. Best calorie density: honey, nuts, peanut butter, canned food, energy bars. 5. Emergency still: pot + plastic sheet + cup can distill small amounts of water.
High-salt food increases thirst — avoid it for emergency stocks. Cooking dry food consumes water — plan for it. The body survives 3 weeks without food, 3 days without water.

1. Plan two escape routes (foot + vehicle) avoiding bridges, tunnels and checkpoints; set rendezvous points along each. 2. Locate yourself: map + compass, three-line intersection. 3. Without a compass: sun by day; North Star / Southern Cross by night. 4. Rivers flow toward people downstream. 5. Record position every 30 minutes. 6. Mark your trail (broken twigs, stone piles) for backtracking.

In fog or darkness, do not move blind — wait for light or use terrain contours. Tell a trusted person your route and timeline; agree on an overdue alarm. Bridges, tunnels and checkpoints are choke points — plan around them.

1. Three fires in a straight line: light at night, smoke by day. 2. SOS ground signal: letters 3–10 m, high contrast, in the open. 3. Signal mirror at aircraft: aim and flash 3 times per group. 4. Registered PLB / satellite beacon: trigger once and leave it on. 5. When rescue arrives: wave bright clothing; at night draw slow circles with a light; stay in place.
Do not waste energy wandering once signaling is set up. Do not start wildfires with signal fires. Check beacon battery expiry dates.

1. Prepare a waterproof card: frequencies, callsigns, code words, listening schedule. 2. Listen 5 minutes at the top of every hour on the agreed frequency. 3. Radios: high ground, slow speech, short bursts. 4. Satellite messenger as backup for beyond-line-of-sight. 5. Mesh/network apps (this app\'s walkie) over local Wi-Fi. 6. Log everything on paper — paper survives.
In wartime, transmitting exposes you — short bursts, then move. Battery discipline: off during non-critical hours. No single channel is reliable — always have two.

1. Silence your devices: location, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi off — or a Faraday bag. 2. Border/checkpoint discipline: power off in advance, split devices among carriers, carry a clean phone. 3. Pay cash for sensitive supplies; skip loyalty cards and fixed schedules. 4. Randomize routes and verify with anti-tracking observation. 5. Sensitive conversations: devices off or bagged, and away from smart speakers.

Every cell tower logs your IMSI and location — assume it is recorded. Car GPS, dashcams and smartwatches are beacons too. A phone that is \"off\" may still be tracked unless the battery is removed or bagged.

1. Tier your power: small (power banks + folding solar for phone/radio), medium (portable power station for lights/medical), large (generator). 2. Solar: angle panels toward the midday sun; overcast days give only 10–30% output. 3. Keep every power bank full; recharge nightly. 4. Generator: run outdoors 5+ m from shelter with a carbon monoxide alarm. 5. Save power: airplane mode, lower brightness, kill background apps.
Lithium batteries in direct sun or under pressure can catch fire. A generator indoors kills — carbon monoxide is odorless. Unstable voltage destroys equipment — use regulators.

1. 4-7-8 breathing: inhale 4 s, hold 7 s, exhale 8 s; repeat 4 rounds. 2. Grounding 5-4-3-2-1: name 5 things you see, 4 you hear, 3 you touch, 2 you smell, 1 you taste. 3. Team psychological first aid: listen without judgment, secure basics (water/food/sleep), assign small tasks. 4. Sleep discipline: guarantee every person 4 continuous hours per 24 h; rotate watch. 5. Caffeine only for critical windows. 6. Panicking teammate: low voice, slow speech, give ONE simple action to do.
Panic spreads faster than any threat — contain it first. Fatigue zeroes judgment — a tired leader makes fatal calls. Breakdowns happen; take turns, do not let everyone collapse at once.

1. Paper emergency card: blood type, allergies, medical history, medications, emergency contacts — one in wallet, one in pack. 2. Keep an encrypted digital copy; tell at least one companion the passphrase. 3. Chronic medication: 30+ days, split across two locations. 4. Triage marking: write injury + time on skin or tape for medics. 5. If blood type is unknown, write UNKNOWN — a wrong type is worse than none.
Battlefield medicine does not wait for you to unlock a phone. Write severe allergies (penicillin) in the most visible place. Medics treat the card, not your memory.

1. EDC (on person): knife, flashlight, lighter, cash, whistle, tourniquet, multitool. 2. 72-hour bag: 3 L water + filter, 3 days food, shelter (tarp/blanket), first aid, comms, spare clothing. 3. Long-term home reserves: two weeks food and water, fuel, generator, medication, copies of key documents. 4. Inspect and rotate stock regularly; replace batteries and expired items. 5. Pack to carry: if you cannot walk 10 km with it, it is too heavy.
A bag that stays at home saves no one — keep one in the vehicle too. Drill: live out of the 72-hour bag once to find its gaps. Two is one, one is none: duplicate the critical items.
